value.0: There you are. The storm with an eye. I watched you cross the yard just now and found nothing to correct, which is a strange feeling for a sparring master. The trial halls keep their rhythm again, and every student who drills there owes you more than they'll ever know. Spar with me sometime. I want to lose properly.

Drop the rear shoulder. Better. Now hear me plainly: the storm form eats half-trained wrists for breakfast. Finish everything the lightsaber still has to teach you, every last cut of it, and then we can talk about what waits in the trial halls.

Stop. Lead foot. You plant it like a fence post, and Saber Storm never plants, it pours. Better. I'm Talan Rees. I ran the storm drills in the Jedi Enclave Trial Halls east of here on Dantooine, until my own students barred the doors on me. Six adepts hold the outer ring now, drilling the form with no restraint and no instructor. Put them down and bring me the Saber Storm Enclave Trial Slate they drill from. That slate is lesson one, and they have been reading it wrong.
Ha. Good answer. Watch the outer ring's floor, it's scored from years of drills and it will catch a dragging heel. Six adepts, then the slate, then me. And tuck that elbow. You were doing it again.

Continuous offense. The blade never stops and the feet never root. Most duelists strike, reset, strike, and a good opponent lives in that reset. The storm attacks out of the reset itself, so there is no seam to counter. Done right, your opponent is fighting weather. Done wrong, you cut off your own line of retreat. My students are doing it wrong.

The trial halls stand east of the enclave courts, here on Dantooine. The key I'll put in your hand unseals their doors; I cut it myself the day they locked me out. Once you're through, follow the sound. Saber work at all hours. Nobody drills that long without hurting somebody.

Mine, once. Students who loved the fury and skipped the footwork. Six of them hold the outer ring, and they fight like the form itself: fast, relentless, no respect for a yield. Don't offer one. They stopped honoring the tap-out months ago.
Outer ring. Six adepts. The Enclave Trial Slate they drill from. The halls won't get quieter while you stretch.
That's the slate under your arm, or I've forgotten the weight of it. Let me see.

Scored, scuffed, whole. I wrote my first storm drills on this slate, you know. The outer ring is clear, and you've earned the second lesson once you've caught your breath. Your footwork is already better. I noticed before you did.

Back straight. There. The outer ring is yours, so we move inward. Five specialists hold the middle ring of the trial halls, my old seconds, the ones who taught the adepts everything reckless they know. They've locked a kyber shard into the drill array to push the form past what a body should give. Break their line, pull the Saber Storm Kyber Focus Shard, and bring it to me before it ruins another set of wrists.
Now that's tempo. Go. The middle ring's pillars throw long shadows and the specialists like to cut from them, so keep your eyes soft and your feet softer. Bring me that shard still warm.

Control. Adepts flail; specialists place every cut. Five of them rotating as one line is a wall of edges, and they will trade you strike for strike without tiring, because the shard drives the drill array and the array never calls rest.

A cut of kyber tuned to a saber's hum. In the trial array it sets tempo, like a metronome that argues back. We used it to teach rhythm. They use it to erase the pause where judgment lives. Pull it, and the middle ring goes quiet.

Don't chase. Five blades want you overextended, and the storm punishes a planted foot worst of all. Move through them, not at them. Also, drink water before you go in. Nobody thinks of it and everybody regrets it.
Five specialists in the middle ring, and the Kyber Focus Shard still setting their tempo. Every hour it hums, they drill deeper into the mistake.
You're carrying a hum I haven't heard in a year. That's the shard. Hand it over before it syncs to your heartbeat. That is not a joke.

There it is. Warm, like I said. I'll cage it in the resonance box where it belongs. The middle ring is silent for the first time in months, and the silence is yours. Rest the wrists. The next lesson does not share.

Shoulders down. Both. Listen close, because this is where I stop grading and start worrying. Past the middle ring stands the third door, and behind it waits the warden, my finest student and my loudest mistake. She carries the Saber Storm Fractured Trial Sigil, the seal that once opened every ring in these halls. I want her stopped and I want the sigil back. And you do not go through that door with fewer than three blades. Trials above the third ring were always taken in threes. Enclave rule, my rule, and the only one she never broke until she did.

That's the first answer you've given me that needed no correction. When she opens, she opens with everything, so the three of you weather that first minute and the drill turns yours. Bring back the sigil. Bring back all three of you.

Because the storm devours a lone opponent. That is its whole design. Two guard the seams while one presses; that is how the high trials have always been survived. The warden has retired finer form than yours one bout at a time, and she does it politely. Bring two blades you trust with your life, because that's the stake on the table.

It cracked the day she sealed the halls. A trial sigil answers to the enclave council, and it split rather than answer to her. She wears it anyway. Broken authority still has the shape of authority, if nobody looks too closely.

My finest student. She passed every drill I set before I finished setting it. When the storm took the others, she didn't rage like the adepts or calculate like the specialists. She simply closed the third door and said the form deserved better students than the Order sends. She isn't wrong about everything. Stop her anyway.
The third door stays shut and the warden still wears the Fractured Trial Sigil. Three blades, one bad first minute, then the drill turns. Do not go in alone. I will know.
The third door stands open. I felt it from here; don't ask how. Show me the sigil.

She always fought like that. Give me a moment with this one. ... All right. The council can mend the sigil or mourn it; that's their drill, not ours. You held the seam work through her opening minute, and that isn't a thing I can teach, only witness. Two rings left. The inner circle knows you're coming.

You're standing squarer. Good. You'll need it. Four remain past the third door, my inner circle, the students I trained to examine everyone else. They hold the high ring and the Saber Storm Council Trial Chit, the token the council stamps when a form is judged safe to teach. Nothing about their storm is safe to teach. Put all four down and carry the chit back to daylight. Take company in with you if you can get it. The circle examines whoever walks in, and they grade harshly.

Ha! Save the confidence, spend the footwork. The high ring is round and rimless, and stepping out means a long drop into the meditation garden, which has never helped anyone meditate. Four blades. One chit. Class dismissed.

A slug of bronzium stamped by the enclave council, and it means this form may be passed on. It is the difference between a discipline and a hazard. While the inner circle holds it, they may teach whoever survives long enough to learn. That is how the storm spread through these halls in the first place.

Like examiners. They test you one at a time until they find the flaw, then all four press it at once. Everyone has the flaw, mind you. You. Me. The trick is knowing yours and folding it behind your guard before they finish the survey.

I did. Proudest work I ever ruined. An examiner must out-fence anyone she grades, so I built four of the best and never asked what happens when examiners stop answering to anyone. Now you're the answer. Sorry about that.
Four examiners in the high ring, and the Council Trial Chit still in their keeping. They have had time to study how the warden fell. Assume they learned from it.
The high ring is empty. All four. I would make you narrate every exchange if that chit weren't more urgent. Well?

Filed and witnessed. The council will want to reissue this under a better custodian, and I intend to nominate you, which should horrify us both. One door remains, and the storm itself behind it. Rest first. That is not advice. It is a drill instruction.

No corrections today. That isn't praise; it's that I can't find anything left to fix from the outside. What's left is behind the last door of the trial halls. The master waits there, and I won't dress it up: the storm you've learned piece by piece, he wields whole. Continuous offense with no eye, no pause, no floor. Beat him, and the form is yours by every law the enclave keeps. His defeat is the only proof I need. But the storm has never spared a lone opponent, and it will not start with you. Bring two blades you'd trust in a storm, because that is exactly where you're taking them.

Then it's a true trial, witnessed and chalked. Weather his first storm, guard each other's seams, and when the rhythm falters, that isn't him tiring. It's him testing. Press anyway. I'll be listening for the quiet.

My first student, and my sparring partner every dawn for eleven years. He mastered the storm before anyone had named it, and it never let him go. He didn't seal these halls out of malice. He sealed them because he believes the form should end with him. Prove it ends with you instead.

Every storm the rest of us make has a center, a still point where the duelist actually lives. Find it and you've found the man. His has none. He is offense with nothing at the middle, and that is the tragedy and the technique both. Three of you means three centers. He cannot erase what he does not have.

Then I chalk the ring, take down the blade hanging on that wall, and finish my own failed lesson at last. But I've watched your footwork since the day I first corrected it, and I'm not oiling that hilt yet. When it gets loud in there, fall back on the drills. They live in your feet now.
The last door waits, and the master behind it. Three blades, no fewer. The storm without an eye does not tire, so plan for the long minute, and then the longer one.
The halls are quiet. Truly quiet. I haven't heard them like this since before he sealed the doors. Tell me it's done.

Then the form lives, and it lives in someone who plants nothing and stays rooted anyway. He would have hated that sentence and been proud of you all the same. The rings will be rechalked and your name written over the storm drills where mine used to sit. Saber Storm is yours now. Teach it better than I did.
Walk me through the drill again.
Adjust my stance all you like. I'm in.
What is Saber Storm, exactly?
How do I get into the trial halls?
Who are these adepts?
Not yet. My form isn't ready.
Here. One trial slate, hard won.
Go back. I had another question.
Middle ring, five blades, one shard. I'm gone.
What makes the specialists different?
What is this focus shard?
Any advice for the middle ring?
Not yet. I need more time on the drills.
Here's your shard. It hummed at me the entire walk back.
Back up. I'm not done asking.
I'll find two blades worth trusting and take the third door.
Why three blades for one warden?
What happened to the sigil?
Tell me about the warden.
Not until the right blades stand beside me.
The Fractured Trial Sigil. She fought like you taught her.
Let's go over the high ring again.
Then examine me. I'll be in the high ring.
What is this council chit?
How does the inner circle fight?
You trained them to test students?
Not today. I know my flaw, and it needs work.
The Council Trial Chit. They graded me. I disagreed.
Say the whole of it once more.
We'll take the last door together. All three of us.
Who is the master?
No eye to the storm. What does that mean for me?
And if the three of us fall?
Not yet. The blades I trust aren't on Dantooine today.
It's done. The storm has an eye now. Me.
